front: Uai, ocê não vem hoje não?
pronunciation: WAHY, oh-SEH NOWNG VENG OH-zhee NOWNG?
back: Hey, aren't you coming today?
context: 'Uai' is the iconic Minas interjection of surprise or emphasis. 'Ocê' (and 'cê') = você. The double 'não' is typical Brazilian negation.

front: Me passa aquele trem ali em cima da mesa.
pronunciation: mee PAH-sah ah-KEH-lee TRENG ah-LEE eng SEE-mah dah MEH-zah.
back: Pass me that thing over there on the table.
context: In Minas, 'trem' (train) means 'thing' and can refer to almost anything: objects, situations, food.

front: Esse pão de queijo tá bão demais, sô!
pronunciation: EH-see POWNG jee KAY-zhoo TAH BOWNG jee-MAHYS, SOH!
back: This cheese bread is really good, man!
context: 'Bão' = bom. 'Demais' = very, really (not 'too much'). 'Sô' (from 'senhor') is a friendly filler, like 'man' or 'mate'.

front: Nó, que trem bão!
pronunciation: NOH, keh TRENG BOWNG!
back: Wow, what a great thing!
context: 'Nó!' is a shortened 'Nossa!' (from 'Nossa Senhora!'), the classic mineiro exclamation.

front: Nossinhora, cê viu o tamanho da fila?
pronunciation: noh-see-NYOH-rah, SEH VEE-oo oo tah-MAH-nyoo dah FEE-lah?
back: Holy cow, did you see the size of the line?
context: 'Nossinhora' = 'Nossa Senhora' (Our Lady) run together. Mineiros swallow syllables in fast speech.

front: Pó pô pô?
pronunciation: POH POH POH?
back: Can I put in some coffee powder?
context: Famous mineirês joke: 'Pode pôr pó?' (may I put coffee powder in?) shrunk to three syllables. Minas speech drops final syllables.

front: Ondé quié o banheiro?
pronunciation: ohn-DEH kee-EH oo bah-NYAY-roo?
back: Where's the bathroom?
context: 'Ondé quié' = 'Onde é que é' contracted. Mineiro speech merges words across their boundaries.

front: Cadê ocê? Tô te esperando faz meia hora!
pronunciation: kah-DEH oh-SEH? TOH chee ehs-peh-RAHN-doo FAHZ MAY-ah OH-rah!
back: Where are you? I've been waiting for you for half an hour!
context: 'Cadê' (where is) is Brazil-wide; 'tô' = estou. 'Faz meia hora' = for half an hour.

front: Põe só um cadinho de açúcar no meu café.
pronunciation: POYNG SOH oong kah-JEE-nyoo jee ah-SOO-kahr noo MEH-oo kah-FEH.
back: Just put a tiny bit of sugar in my coffee.
context: 'Cadinho' / 'cadim' = 'bocadinho' (a little bit). Mineiros also say 'um tiquim' (um tiquinho).

front: A casa dela é pertim, dá pra ir a pé.
pronunciation: ah KAH-zah DEH-lah EH pehr-CHEENG, DAH prah EER ah PEH.
back: Her house is really close; you can walk there.
context: The mineiro diminutive often ends in '-im' instead of '-inho': pertim (pertinho), cafezim (cafezinho), rapidim (rapidinho).

front: Bora tomar um cafezim antes de sair?
pronunciation: BOH-rah toh-MAHR oong kah-feh-ZEENG AHN-cheez jee sah-EER?
back: Shall we have a little coffee before we go?
context: 'Bora' = 'vamos embora' (let's go). Offering coffee is a sacred ritual of mineiro hospitality.

front: Ocê é doido, sô? Vai sair nessa chuva?
pronunciation: oh-SEH EH DOY-doo, SOH? VAHY sah-EER NEH-sah SHOO-vah?
back: Are you crazy, man? You're going out in this rain?
context: 'Doido' (crazy) is used affectionately. Mineiro rhythm makes it sound more caring than aggressive.

front: Esse menino é doidimais da conta.
pronunciation: EH-see meh-NEE-noo EH doy-jee-MAHYZ dah KOHN-tah.
back: That boy is completely nuts.
context: 'Doidimais' = 'doido demais'. 'Da conta' intensifies: 'bom da conta', 'difícil da conta' = extremely good/difficult.

front: Arreda pra lá, deixa eu sentar também.
pronunciation: ah-RREH-dah prah LAH, DAY-shah EH-oo sehn-TAHR tahm-BENG.
back: Scoot over, let me sit down too.
context: 'Arredar' = to move aside, an old Portuguese verb still alive in Minas and the countryside.

front: O almoço é um mexidão com o que sobrou de ontem.
pronunciation: oo ahl-MOH-soo EH oong meh-shee-DOWNG kohng oo keh soh-BROH jee ohn-TENG.
back: Lunch is a scramble made of yesterday's leftovers.
context: 'Mexidão' = rice, beans, eggs and leftovers stir-fried together: thrifty mineiro comfort food.

front: Ô trem bom é comida feita no fogão a lenha!
pronunciation: OH TRENG BOHNG EH koh-MEE-dah FAY-tah noo foh-GOWNG ah LEH-nyah!
back: There's nothing like food cooked on a wood stove!
context: 'Fogão a lenha' (wood-burning stove) is a symbol of Minas cooking and farm life.

front: Mineiro come quieto.
pronunciation: mee-NAY-roo KOH-mee kee-EH-too.
back: Mineiros keep their cards close to their chest.
context: Saying (literally 'mineiros eat quietly'): people from Minas are discreet, don't brag and quietly get what they want.

front: Mineiro não perde o trem.
pronunciation: mee-NAY-roo NOWNG PEHR-jee oo TRENG.
back: A mineiro never misses the train.
context: Saying about mineiro caution and punctuality: they arrive early and never miss an opportunity. A pun on 'trem'.

front: Vou ali e já volto, uai.
pronunciation: VOH ah-LEE ee ZHAH VOHL-too, WAHY.
back: I'm just popping out and I'll be right back.
context: 'Ali' and 'já volto' are famously vague in Brazil. 'Uai' at the end just adds a casual, matter-of-fact tone.

front: Tá vendo esse morro? Minha fazenda fica pra lá das bandas de Diamantina.
pronunciation: TAH VEHN-doo EH-see MOH-rroo? MEE-nyah fah-ZEHN-dah FEE-kah prah LAH dahz BAHN-dahz jee jee-ah-mahn-CHEE-nah.
back: See that hill? My farm is out past Diamantina way.
context: 'Pras bandas de' = in the area of, out toward. Minas is all hills ('morros') and mountains.

front: Fio, vem cá que a vó tá te chamando.
pronunciation: FEE-oo, VENG KAH keh ah VOH TAH chee shah-MAHN-doo.
back: Son, come here, Grandma's calling you.
context: 'Fio' / 'fia' = filho/filha (the 'lh' becomes 'i' in rural Minas speech). Used affectionately for any young person.

front: Num sei não, sô, acho que vai dar chuva.
pronunciation: NOONG SAY NOWNG, SOH, AH-shoo keh VAHY DAHR SHOO-vah.
back: I don't really know, man, I think it's going to rain.
context: 'Num' = 'não' before a verb in fast speech. 'Vai dar chuva' = it's going to rain.

front: O doce de leite da minha tia é coisa de outro mundo.
pronunciation: oo DOH-see jee LAY-chee dah MEE-nyah CHEE-ah EH KOY-zah jee OH-troo MOON-doo.
back: My aunt's dulce de leche is out of this world.
context: Minas is famous for 'doce de leite', cheeses and 'goiabada'. 'Coisa de outro mundo' = out of this world.

front: Queijo com goiabada é o famoso Romeu e Julieta.
pronunciation: KAY-zhoo kohng goy-ah-BAH-dah EH oo fah-MOH-zoo rroh-MEH-oo ee zhoo-lee-EH-tah.
back: Cheese with guava paste is the famous Romeo and Juliet.
context: The classic mineiro dessert: Minas cheese with guava paste, a perfect couple like Romeo and Juliet.

front: Quietim aí, que o nenê tá dormindo.
pronunciation: kee-eh-CHEENG ah-EE, keh oo neh-NEH TAH dohr-MEEN-doo.
back: Keep quiet there, the baby's sleeping.
context: 'Quietim' = 'quietinho'. Diminutives soften commands, very mineiro.

front: Tô morrendo de saudade do meu interior.
pronunciation: TOH moh-RREHN-doo jee sow-DAH-jee doo MEH-oo een-teh-ree-OHR.
back: I really miss my hometown in the countryside.
context: 'Interior' = small-town countryside. Mineiros in big cities are famously nostalgic for their 'roça' (farm).

front: Ê laiá, lá vem o ônibus atrasado de novo!
pronunciation: EH lah-YAH, LAH VENG oo OH-nee-boos ah-trah-ZAH-doo jee NOH-voo!
back: Oh boy, here comes the late bus again!
context: 'Ê laiá' expresses resignation or mild exasperation. Also heard as 'ê lasqueira'.

front: Ele é mineiro: fala devagar, pensa muito e desconfia de tudo.
pronunciation: EH-lee EH mee-NAY-roo: FAH-lah jee-vah-GAHR, PEHN-sah MOOY-too ee jehs-kohn-FEE-ah jee TOO-doo.
back: He's from Minas: he talks slowly, thinks a lot and is suspicious of everything.
context: The affectionate stereotype of the mineiro: cautious, calm and wary ('desconfiado').

front: Cê qué que eu esquento a comida procê?
pronunciation: SEH KEH keh EH-oo ehs-KEHN-too ah koh-MEE-dah proh-SEH?
back: Do you want me to heat up the food for you?
context: 'Qué' = quer; 'procê' = para você. Feeding guests is central to mineiro hospitality.

front: Vamo chegano, a casa é sua!
pronunciation: VAH-moo sheh-GAH-noo, ah KAH-zah EH SOO-ah!
back: Come on in, make yourself at home!
context: Dropping the 'd' in gerunds ('chegano' = chegando) is common in Minas and much of Brazil. 'A casa é sua' = make yourself at home.

front: Já almoçou? Senta aí que tem comida pra todo mundo.
pronunciation: ZHAH ahl-moh-SOH? SEHN-tah ah-EE keh teng koh-MEE-dah prah TOH-doo MOON-doo.
back: Have you had lunch? Sit down, there's food for everyone.
context: Typical mineiro welcome: refusing food may sound impolite.

front: O sotaque mineiro tem o 'r' caipira, puxado no fim das palavras.
pronunciation: oo soh-TAH-kee mee-NAY-roo teng oo EH-rree kahy-PEE-rah, poo-SHAH-doo noo FEENG dahs pah-LAH-vrahs.
back: The mineiro accent has the countryside 'r', curled at the end of words.
context: The 'r caipira' (retroflex r, like American English) appears in parts of Minas, São Paulo and Goiás, in words like 'porta' and 'calor'.

front: Esse caminho é longe pra chuchu.
pronunciation: EH-see kah-MEE-nyoo EH LOHN-zhee prah shoo-SHOO.
back: This road is really long.
context: 'Pra chuchu' = a lot, very (chuchu is a vegetable). Common all over Brazil, but loved in Minas.

front: Pode ficar sossegado, que eu resolvo esse trem.
pronunciation: POH-jee fee-KAHR soh-seh-GAH-doo, keh EH-oo rreh-ZOHL-voo EH-see TRENG.
back: Don't worry, I'll sort this thing out.
context: 'Ficar sossegado' = to relax, not worry. Here 'esse trem' = this situation or problem.

front: Uai, mas ninguém me avisou que era hoje!
pronunciation: WAHY, mahz neen-GENG mee ah-vee-ZOH keh EH-rah OH-zhee!
back: Hey, but nobody told me it was today!
context: 'Uai' expressing indignant surprise. It's so linked to Minas that it works like a regional signature.
